cells.text: General-domain encyclopedic fact verification: claims are verified against the introductory sections of Wikipedia pages (June 2017 dump, ~50,000 popular pages).

Biomedical / scientific literature: 1,409 expert-written claims verified against a 5,183-abstract corpus of scientific abstracts (seed, co-cited and distractor), plus a COVID-19 extension over CORD-19.

Synthetic claims: annotators wrote claims about a single fact from sampled Wikipedia sentences, then produced meaning-altering mutations (paraphrase, negation, entity/relation substitution, generalization/specialization). Mean claim length 9.4 tokens.

Natural, expert-written atomic scientific claims derived from citances (citation sentences) in scientific articles, verifiable from a single source; compound claims were split into atomic ones. The paper explicitly contrasts this with FEVER's synthetic mutations.

Sentence-level: a combination of Wikipedia sentences (possibly spanning multiple documents/pages) must be returned for SUPPORTED/REFUTED; a prediction counts only if the full sentence set is selected (multi-hop evidence from more than one document possible). NEI claims have no annotated evidence.

Two-level: abstract-level evidence (evidence abstracts retrieved from the corpus, labeled SUPPORTS/REFUTES/NO INFO) and sentence-level rationales defined as the minimal set of sentences in an abstract that imply the claim; evaluation done at both abstract and sentence granularity.

Not directly comparable. FEVER reports 3-way label accuracy (and sentence-level evidence F1 / 'fully supported' proportion) on a balanced train/dev/test over Wikipedia with an NEI class; its headline figures (e.g. 31.87% with gold evidence, 50.91% without) use a different task definition, different corpus and a sentence-set evidence requirement.

input.question: Compare fever and scifact in terms of domain, claim construction, evidence unit. Can their reported scores be compared directly?

cells.text: General-domain encyclopedic fact verification: claims are verified against the introductory sections of Wikipedia pages, built from a June 2017 Wikipedia dump and sampled from ~50,000 popular pages.

Specialized scientific/biomedical domain: claims about scientific findings, verified against abstracts from well-regarded journals (Cell, Nature, JAMA, BMJ), drawn from S2ORC and covering diverse biomedical topics; includes a COVID-19 case study against CORD-19.

Two-stage human construction: annotators wrote claims from randomly sampled Wikipedia sentences (single piece of information about the page entity), then claims were mutated (paraphrase, negation, entity/relation substitution, generalization/specialization), yielding mean length 9.4 tokens.

Claims are expert-written reformulations of naturally occurring citation sentences (citances) from citing papers, into 'atomic scientific claims' without sight of the cited abstract; REFUTES examples were created by an NLP expert writing negations.

Evidence is a set of sentences (potentially spanning multiple Wikipedia pages) that jointly justify SUPPORTED/REFUTED labels; NOT ENOUGH INFO claims have no annotated evidence; evidence F1 is computed over predicted sentence sets, with 17.47% F1 reported for the full pipeline.

Evidence is a rationale: up to three mutually exclusive, mostly contiguous sentences within a single cited abstract (28 rationales non-contiguous), labeled at abstract level as SUPPORTS/REFUTES/NO INFO; 63% of cited abstracts contain evidence.

FEVER scores are label accuracy reported both with and without evidence, plus evidence sentence F1; the best system reaches 31.87% when evidence must be correct versus 50.91% ignoring evidence. These figures are not comparable to SCIFACT numbers because the evidence retrieval setting differs: FEVER requires open retrieval over ~50,000 Wikipedia pages, where the document retrieval component often fails (58.27% of analyzed errors) and a much larger, automatically altered claim pool is used.

SCIFACT scores are reported under distinct settings (Oracle abstract, Oracle rationale, Open; abstract-level label F1 and sentence-level rationale P/R/F1), and the paper itself flags that oracle-abstract F1 only 'roughly' matches label accuracy. Conditions differ from FEVER: a small 1,409-claim set over 5,183 abstracts, claims/abstracts often already linked by citations, and top-k=3 retrieval, so its numbers cannot be placed on the same scale as FEVER's open-Wikipedia results; the only shared design element is that FEVER is used as out-of-domain pretraining data.
